correctness.rationale: Proof reconstructs the positive invariant box, exact log-Jacobian derivative and strictly subunit row-sum bound for every 0<h<=1, yielding global exponential convergence by Banach. For every h>1 the scalar map has fixed-point derivative below -1 and the sign-change argument for f² yields a positive two-cycle. For h=2 the original two-gene diagonal orbit and its full-plane two multipliers are exactly checked. The included SymPy checker confirmed the critical identities; finite iterations are only corroboration.

originality.rationale: The inspected complete source articles give selected high-Hill numerical/topological dynamics, an absorbing region, or chaos at h>=3. None of those results implies a global all-network Hill <=1 contraction with an explicit rate and the sharp h>1 two-cycle boundary. An older original paper is inaccessible and is a named historical risk.
residual_risks: The full text of the original 2007 Andrecut–Kauffman paper could not be examined despite open-access and authorized institutional attempts; older priority could be understated.
A 2019 analysis by Sharma and Saha was found only at abstract level and may contain uninspected low-exponent statements.

General contraction theory in logarithmic coordinates is classical; novelty is asserted for this exact sharp finite-network model theorem and explicit stable dimer boundary, not for the method itself.
Some other unpublished or nonindexed literature could imply the special case via a stronger nonlinear contraction theorem.

value.rationale: The sharp, dimension-independent Hill threshold separates an unconditionally globally convergent inhibitory response from possible oscillation. It resolves natural uncertainty in monomeric versus dimeric gene-expression maps, supplies an explicit computable convergence factor, and constructs a stable two-gene periodic orbit proving the transition is dynamically substantive. The result is restricted to a scientifically motivated reciprocal-Hill inhibition class and does not claim a broad biochemical theorem.
